HYPOTHESIS (answer to: "For which domains do the effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies?"):

Original-study effect sizes are larger than replication-study effect sizes in every domain, but the original-vs-replication gap is largest in the Social (psychology) domain — where replications retain on average only ~28% of the original effect size (mean relative_es = 0.28) and only 11.8% of replications match or exceed the original — and smallest in the Experimental Economics domain (replications retain ~66%, mean relative_es = 0.66). At the coarser project level, the same pattern holds: effect sizes shrink more from original to replication in the Psychology project (mean relative_es ≈ 0.39) than in the Experimental Economics project (≈ 0.66).

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE — per-domain tables (86 paired original–replication rows; 0 missing in all ES columns):

Discipline level (primary):
| Domain | n | mean ro | mean rr | mean fiso | mean fisr | paired diff (Fisher-z) | paired diff (raw r) | mean relative_es (rr/ro) | frac rr>ro | frac rr<0 | Wilcoxon p (Fisher-z diff) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cognitive | 34 | 0.534 | 0.285 | 0.627 | 0.338 | +0.289 | +0.249 | 0.509 | 17.6% | 14.7% | <0.0001 |
| Economics | 18 | 0.474 | 0.278 | 0.572 | 0.307 | +0.266 | +0.196 | 0.657 | 16.7% | 16.7% | 0.0008 |
| Social | 34 | 0.346 | 0.123 | 0.373 | 0.141 | +0.233 | +0.223 | 0.278 | 11.8% | 29.4% | <0.0001 |

Project level (2-level): Psychology (n=68): mean ro 0.440 vs rr 0.204, mean relative_es 0.394, 14.7% rr>ro; Experimental Economics (n=18): mean ro 0.474 vs rr 0.278, mean relative_es 0.657, 16.7% rr>ro. In all four domain groups the paired difference ro−rr (and fiso−fisr) is positive and significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank, two-sided; all p ≤ 0.0016).

Cross-domain significance of the gap: Kruskal-Wallis on relative_es across the 3 disciplines: H=8.34, p=0.0155. Pairwise Mann-Whitney: Social < Cognitive (p=0.015), Social < Economics (p=0.019), Cognitive ≈ Economics (p=0.56).

Dual-scale sensitivity check: the ranking of domains by *mean absolute* paired difference is scale-dependent (Fisher-z: Cognitive 0.289 > Economics 0.266 > Social 0.233; raw r: Cognitive 0.249 > Social 0.223 > Economics 0.196), because Social's small raw r values compress the Fisher-z difference. However, the scale-free relative_es and the direction counts are consistent across all checks and identify Social as the domain with the largest original-vs-replication gap. Excluding the 18 sign-reversed replications (rr<0; 29.4% of Social rows) does not change the conclusion: mean relative_es becomes Cognitive 0.673, Economics 0.828, Social 0.468 — Social still retains the least.

Limitations: small per-domain N (Economics n=18); inferential tests are exploratory; negative replications (opposite direction) inflate absolute differences, so I report both with and without them; the two-level and three-level domain views are perfectly nested (Cognitive+Social = Psychology), so the two statements are consistent views of the same data.

payload.workflow: Loaded the 86-row joined CSV (0 missing in ro/rr/fiso/fisr/relative_es). Computed row-level paired differences (fiso-fisr on Fisher-z scale and ro-rr on raw correlation scale) and per-domain means, medians, and direction counts (fraction of pairs with rr>ro) for each discipline (Cognitive n=34, Social n=34, Economics n=18) and each project (Psychology n=68, Experimental Economics n=18). Tested the paired differences with Wilcoxon signed-rank per domain (all significant, p <= 0.0016) and compared domains via Kruskal-Wallis (H=8.34, p=0.016) and pairwise Mann-Whitney on relative_es. Ran a dual-scale sensitivity check (raw r vs Fisher-z, noting the mean-difference ranking is scale-dependent while relative_es is not) and a sensitivity analysis excluding the 18 sign-reversed replications (rr<0), which left the Social-domain gap the largest.
